facts.t: The All India Judicial Service has been recommended since 1986
facts.d: The 116th Law Commission Report proposed it, the Malimath Committee endorsed it, and the 21st Law Commission urged urgent action. Article 312 already empowers Parliament to create it. Four decades on, it does not exist.

facts.t: High Courts, not governments, control the district judiciary
facts.d: Article 235 vests control over posting, promotion and discipline of subordinate judges in the High Court. It is the strongest structural protection for judicial independence at the level where most citizens actually meet the courts.

facts.t: Three years at the Bar is now mandatory again
facts.d: The requirement of prior practice before entering judicial service was removed in the 1990s to attract fresh graduates, then restored — on the reasoning that courtroom experience cannot be taught in an academy.

bank.q: Control over the subordinate judiciary vests in:
bank.e: Article 235 places control with the High Court — a deliberate insulation of the district judiciary from executive influence.

bank.q: With reference to Articles 233 and 234, consider the following statements:
s: District Judges are appointed by the Governor in consultation with the High Court.
Other subordinate judges are appointed by the Governor in consultation with the High Court and the State Public Service Commission.
Direct recruitment to the post of District Judge requires seven years' practice.
bank.e: All three are correct — the seven-year requirement governs direct entry from the Bar into the senior cadre.

bank.q: Match List I (case) with List II (contribution):
pairs: 1. Delay in appointments violates access to justice
2. Norms for service conditions, fixed tenure and training
4. Fixed calendar deadlines for judicial recruitment
bank.e: Service-condition norms, the recruitment calendar in Malik Mazhar Sultan, the access-to-justice holding in 2019, and the direction to set up judicial academies.

bank.q: Which one of the following is NOT an argument advanced for the All India Judicial Service?
o: Uniformity of standards and merit-based selection
Strengthening the High Court's oversight role
A better career pipeline with common training
bank.e: Undermining High Court oversight is an argument against the AIJS, not for it.

bank.as: The subordinate judiciary is described as the first line of defence.
bank.rs: It carries around 87% of India's total pendency and is where most citizens encounter the justice system.
bank.e: Both true and the Reason explains the Assertion — which is why vacancies of 20 to 30% at this level matter more than anywhere else.

bank.q: Which Law Commission report first recommended an All India Judicial Service?
bank.e: The 116th Report of 1986. The 214th concerns higher judicial appointments and the 267th hate speech.

bank.q: Consider the following objections to the All India Judicial Service:
s: It infringes state powers under Articles 233 and 234.
It raises language and local-law difficulties.
It requires a constitutional amendment to Article 312.
bank.e: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Article 312 already empowers Parliament to create such a service — no amendment is needed.

bank.q: All of the following are identified as problems in subordinate judicial recruitment EXCEPT:
o: Inconsistent exams and syllabi across states
Vacancies of 20 to 30% in many states
Uniform institutionalised academy training across all states
Political and executive interference in some states
bank.e: Such training is not institutionalised across states — its absence is listed among the training gaps.

bank.q: Vacancy in the subordinate judiciary stands at approximately:
bank.e: Around 23%, against a service that carries 87% of national pendency.

bank.q: With reference to the structure of state judicial services, consider the following:
s: Each state maintains its own judicial service.
The service is split between a regular and a higher judicial service.
High Court judges are appointed exclusively from the state judicial service.
bank.e: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. High Court judges come both from the state judicial service and from the state High Court Bar.
